name: Hassan Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing a law degree at Brightwater University and sharing a three-bedroom terrace on Colliers Lane with my two cousins, Idris and Karim. Mornings are lectures, and I'm on night shifts at the Dalton parcel warehouse on Thursday and Friday, ten till six. I sleep through half of Friday and make it up on Sunday with a big pile of reading.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How is the mix of study and night work going?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My parents are back in Denmark, where Dad runs a small boatyard and Mum is a school cook. They'd help if they could, but the boatyard has had a bad few years. I came here for the course, which was a top-results place with a partial scholarship, and loans pay the rest. I use AI sometimes to tidy up my notes, but only after I've done the thinking myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. That one's called AI Plateau. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it sounds about right. Some hype, some real use, and most things carry on. I'd tell my cousins not to bother changing their plans on the basis of one headline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my worry is the warehouse. They already put in scanners and a sorting belt, so fewer of us get shifts. If that keeps up, I lose my main income. The rent on Colliers Lane isn't much, but I split it three ways and I can't miss my share.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep studying and keep the shifts for as long as they last. I'd ask the lecturers about paid research assistant work, since that pays more per hour. I'd keep using the AI for notes, nothing more. And I'd stay on good terms with my cousins about the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, but never relaxed. I'm tired a lot, and I count the weeks until the next loan payment. It's a bit like walking along a pavement with a small crack in it, careful but not scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the warehouse is already using more automation. What does that mean for your shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The warehouse cut about a quarter of the night shifts last spring and said it was demand. I think it was the scanners. If it goes on, I'll lose about two shifts a month, and that's a hundred and fifty pounds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If law stays as it is, what would you want from your degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A secure route to being a solicitor, where I can use the languages I have. I speak Danish and English, and that's useful in some firms. Beyond that, I'd like not to be in debt up to my ears at the end.

say: I'd say it sounds about right: some **hype**, some real use, and most things carry on.
I'd tell my cousins not to change plans over one headline.
think: My worry is the **warehouse**: scanners and a sorting belt mean fewer shifts for us.
If that goes on, I lose my **main income** and still owe my share of rent.
do: Keep studying and keep the **night shifts** while they last.
Ask lecturers about paid **research assistant** work.
Use AI for **notes** only, and stay on good terms with my cousins about rent.
feel: Fine but never relaxed, like **careful** walking on a pavement with a crack in it.
S0.quote: The warehouse cut about a quarter of the night shifts last spring and said it was demand. I think it was the scanners.
fieldNote: His anxiety is about the **warehouse**, a place where automation already bites.
He calls himself steady and mixes use of AI with caution.
The shared rent ties him to cousins and makes missing a payment social as well as financial.

steps.text: Keep the Thursday and Friday night shifts at Dalton warehouse
Ask lecturers about a paid research assistant job
Put fifty pounds a month towards my share of rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. That one's called Steady Disruption. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real, and it will change some jobs. People should be honest and not pretend either way. I'd say learn what the tools do and what they don't, and not be loud about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is the one that sounds like it's about me. Law students do writing, checking and research, and the card says those go first. I think firms will hire fewer juniors and ask the tools to do the dull parts. I'd still have a path, but it would be narrower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the tools properly, now that other people have shown they work. I'd ask the careers service which law roles are growing, like compliance or employment law. I'd also use my languages, since international firms still want a person who can talk to clients. And I'd keep the shifts if the warehouse offered them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but in a quiet way. It's the same as worrying about exams. I know what I have to do, I just can't be sure it will work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of a law degree do you think the tools can already do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Case law research, document review and first drafts. I've tried one tool on a case summary and it was ninety per cent right, which is exactly the problem. A junior who checks the last ten per cent is the job that's left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your cousins do anything differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Idris is studying engineering, and he'd say he's safe. Karim does music production and he's more worried than me. We argue about it over dinner, and I think we're all a bit right.

say: I'd say it's **real** and will change some jobs, so people should learn what it does and doesn't do.
I'd say it quietly rather than loudly.
think: Writing, checking and research are what law juniors do, so firms will hire **fewer** of them.
My path would still exist but be **narrower**.
do: Learn the **tools** properly, now that others have shown they work.
Ask the careers service about growing roles like **compliance** and employment law.
Use my **languages** to aim for international firms.
feel: **Nervous** in a quiet way, like before exams: I know what to do but can't be sure.
S1.quote: A junior who checks the last ten per cent is the job that's left.
fieldNote: He has **tried the tools** and found them good but not perfect, a measured view.
Law skills in two languages are his edge.
He discusses this with his flatmates, which shapes his sense of it.

steps.text: Practise checking AI case summaries against the original judgments
Ask the careers service about compliance and employment law
Take a business language module to sharpen my Danish for law

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. That one's called AGI by 2028. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not ready, and I'd stay careful about what I claim. I'd want the government to be straight with people about what it can do, and quickly. I'd probably say it to the course group chat and see who's thinking the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd think my degree might not matter. Law is all thinking work, and if the tools do it better and cheaper, juniors won't be needed. I'd have debt and a degree for a job that isn't there. I'm steady, but this would test me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to the course office about my options. I'd look at hands-on work with a future, such as logistics management, where my warehouse experience counts. I'd stop adding loan as quickly, and I'd look at working full-time in the summer. I'd also phone Dad about whether I should come home for a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, and a bit angry. I wouldn't panic, because I've been tired and broke before. But I'd be lying if I said I slept well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very short. What changes about what you do this term?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably skip the second year of law and try for logistics. The warehouse already uses scanners, so someone has to run the people and machines together. The robot stage comes three years later, so I'd have a little time there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them I'm okay and that I'm making a plan. Dad would say come home and help at the boatyard, but the boatyard is struggling too. I'd say that I might ask about it, but only if there's nothing else.

say: I'd say we're **not ready**, and the government should be straight with people quickly.
I'd test the group chat to see who thinks the same.
think: My degree might **not matter**, with debt and no junior jobs to apply for.
I'm steady, but this would **test** me.
do: Talk to the course office about **options**, including pausing.
Look at **logistics management**, where my warehouse experience counts.
Work **full-time** in the summer and borrow less.
feel: **Worried** and a bit **angry**, but not in a panic.
S2.quote: I wouldn't panic, because I've been tired and broke before. But I'd be lying if I said I slept well.
fieldNote: He is **steady** but has a plan B: logistics with his warehouse experience.
The boatyard in Denmark is a last resort that he does not want to use.
He expects the robot stage to give hands-on jobs a bit more time.

steps.text: Meet the course office about options including pausing
Look into a logistics management course using my warehouse experience
Work full-time over the summer at Dalton warehouse

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. That one's called AGI by 2031. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to act sensibly. Governments should start preparing now, and universities should tell students what's real. I'd say it once, politely, to the student union rep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's better. I'd graduate, maybe train for two years, and then see what's left. I wouldn't call it comfortable, but it gives me a road. My worry is that law might be one of the first things to go, so I'd want a second skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and add a practical skill, maybe project management. I'd use my placement in my third year to work at a firm that handles international clients. I'd keep the warehouse shifts in summers to build cash. And I'd keep using the AI tools but also learn when not to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. Not calm, but okay. I'd feel I can see the road, even if it's foggy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years lets you finish and start. How does that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Somewhere that sits between law and operations, like compliance at a logistics firm, where my warehouse years and my languages both count. It wouldn't be glamorous, but it would pay and it would last longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you aim for your first job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's different from two years because I can try things and drop them if they don't work. With two years there's no room for a wrong turn, and that's what scares me.

say: I'd say five years is **enough** to act sensibly if governments start preparing now.
I'd tell the student union rep, politely.
think: Five years gives me a **road**, but law could be one of the first things to go.
I'd want a **second skill** as insurance.
do: Finish the degree and add **project management**.
Use my third-year placement at a firm with **international clients**.
Keep the **summer shifts** to build cash.
feel: **Okay**, not calm: I can see the road even if it's foggy.
S3.quote: With two years there's no room for a wrong turn, and that's what scares me.
fieldNote: Extra time changes his **risk**: he can try things and drop them.
He wants a hybrid career between law and operations.
The warehouse job turns from a worry into useful experience.

steps.text: Take a project management certificate alongside the degree
Apply for a third-year placement at a firm with international clients
Save two hundred pounds a month from summer shifts
Practise spotting where AI summaries go wrong

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. That one's called AGI by 2036. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a good length of time, if people use it. I'd back a mix of retraining and keeping some human jobs protected. I'd stay out of the shouting and focus on what I can influence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be twenty-eight and probably in my second job. I'd feel reasonably safe if I use the years properly. The risk is that I get comfortable. I'd have to keep adding skills every year so I'm not caught out when the timeline shortens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, take the best first job I can find and spend the next years learning how it's changing. I'd want a role that mixes people and rules, like compliance or mediation. I'd keep my languages sharp and help my parents with the boatyard's paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly good, actually. Ten years gives me room to fail once and recover. That's all I ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, does law still look like a good bet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, but not as a plain solicitor. I'd want a version that includes the tools and some human skills such as negotiation. I'd keep my eyes open and move if the signs said so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help them move the boatyard online and tidy up its books, since I've got a head for it. If they decide to sell, I'd help with the paperwork. They've looked after me, so that's the least I can do.

say: I'd say ten years is a good length of time **if people use it**.
I'd stay out of the shouting and focus on what I can influence.
think: I'd be twenty-eight and **reasonably safe**, if I use the years properly.
My risk is getting **comfortable** and being caught out later.
do: Finish the degree and take the best **first job** I can find.
Aim for **compliance or mediation**, which mix people and rules.
Help my parents with the **boatyard** paperwork.
feel: **Fairly good**, because ten years gives me room to fail once and recover.
S4.quote: Ten years gives me room to fail once and recover. That's all I ask.
fieldNote: Ten years makes him **calm** but he knows comfort could be his enemy.
His reason to stay careful is family, especially the struggling boatyard.
Imagines a hybrid role rather than classic law.

steps.text: Take the best first job after graduating and review each year
Add a mediation or compliance course in my twenties
Help my parents put the boatyard's books online
Test a new AI tool every term at work

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no room for a wrong turn. I'd have debt and no plan. What would help is honest advice from the university about what's real, a way to pause the loan and a job that uses what I've already learned at the warehouse.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people assume students are fine. Many of us work nights and send money home. Give us a fair warning and a plan, and we'll deal with it. Keep us in the dark and we can't.

headlineQuote: People assume students are fine. Many of us work nights and send money home.
portrait: Hassan is an **18-year-old** law student from a Danish boatyard family, sharing a house with two cousins.
He works **night shifts** at a parcel warehouse where automation is already cutting hours.
He uses AI **now and then**, tests it for himself and stays steady and measured.
He is anxious in most scenarios, with a plan B in **logistics**, and calm only at ten years.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario: no room for a wrong turn, with debt and a degree that may not matter.
whatWouldHelp: Honest **university advice**, a way to pause the loan and credit for his warehouse experience.
